metadata.title: Analysis of the Effects of World Bank Macroeconomic and Management Indicators on Sustainable Education Quality on PISA Scores Using the SHAP Explainable Artificial Intelligence Method

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study builds country-level feature datasets (governance, economic capacity, democracy, and regional categories) and then trains multi-class ML classifiers to assign countries to Low/Medium/High achievement classes for PISA Mathematics, Reading, and Science. Because the analysis is performed on aggregate country indicators rather than student microdata, the paper does not describe the use of PISA sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures. The methodology section focuses on feature scaling, two-stage feature elimination (correlation thresholding and VIF filtering), and model selection using train/test accuracy and class-wise Precision/Recall/F1. For analysts wishing to reproduce or extend this pipeline with student-level PISA microdata, complex survey weights (e.g., student/sampling weights and BRR/jackknife replicates) would need to be applied consistently; however, this paper’s design does not provide weight variable names or a weighting protocol.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are constructed as PISA domain mean scores (PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) that are then discretized into Low/Medium/High classes using fixed score thresholds. The paper does not report any plausible-values (PV) workflow (e.g., Rubin’s rules across PVs), which is consistent with using aggregated mean scores rather than PV-based achievement estimates. For missing data, the paper states that PISA scores were imputed using trend-based interpolation, but it does not specify a formal missing-data handling category (e.g., listwise deletion vs. multiple imputation) or the extent of missingness, so the missing-data strategy is not fully documented for replication.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used country-level indicators for each PISA domain target (PISAM, PISAR, PISAS) and created three separate datasets with the same explanatory features. PISA scores were imputed when unavailable for certain years/countries using trend-based interpolation, and all numerical variables were scaled for comparability. The final modeling feature set was restricted to 13 variables after two-stage feature selection: (i) greedy elimination removing features with |r| >= 0.90 and (ii) iterative VIF elimination removing features with VIF > 7.0. The paper does not report additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., specific country list, year range, or minimum observation counts) in the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA Mathematics (PISAM) mean scores; multi-class Low/Medium/High achievement profile
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best model). Class-based metrics (Precision/Recall/F1): Low 0.97/0.97/0.97 (Support 110); Medium 0.91/0.93/0.92 (Support 107); High 0.96/0.94/0.95 (Support 111). General metrics: Train Accuracy = 1.0; Test Accuracy = 0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC = 0.98–1.00; Macro Avg ≈ 0.93–0.95; Weighted Avg ≈ 0.93–0.95. SHAP reliability: Fidelity 0.95; Faithfulness 0.85.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA Mathematics (PISAM) mean scores the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, Political Stability, Regional category (bloc), and GDP per capita to predict PISAM achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that governance indicators (especially Voice and Accountability and Control of Corruption) form the most salient institutional core, with political stability and regional location further differentiating classes. This indicates that strengthening governance and anti-corruption capacity may be a key policy lever for improving sustainable mathematics performance profiles, though the results are predictive associations at the country level rather than causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA Reading (PISAR) mean scores; multi-class Low/Medium/High achievement profile
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best model). Class-based metrics (Precision/Recall/F1): Low 0.95/0.97/0.96 (Support 108); Medium 0.94/0.84/0.89 (Support 112); High 0.90/0.97/0.93 (Support 108). General metrics: Train Accuracy = 1.0; Test Accuracy = 0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC = 0.98–1.00; Macro Avg ≈ 0.93–0.95; Weighted Avg ≈ 0.93–0.95. SHAP reliability: Fidelity 0.89; Faithfulness 0.92.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA Reading (PISAR) mean scores the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, GDP, GDP per capita, and Regional category (bloc) to predict PISAR achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that the model integrates economic capacity more strongly with the governance core than in mathematics. This indicates that sustainable reading improvements may require pairing governance reforms with targeted investment capacity, while recognizing that the pipeline provides decision-support signals rather than causal guarantees.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA Science (PISAS) mean scores; multi-class Low/Medium/High achievement profile
main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (best model). Class-based metrics (Precision/Recall/F1): Low 0.95/1.00/0.97 (Support 107); Medium 0.95/0.90/0.92 (Support 116); High 0.94/0.95/0.95 (Support 105). General metrics: Train Accuracy = 1.0; Test Accuracy = 0.93–0.95; ROC-AUC = 0.98–1.00; Macro Avg ≈ 0.93–0.95; Weighted Avg ≈ 0.93–0.95. SHAP reliability: Fidelity 0.89; Faithfulness 0.89.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA Science (PISAS) mean scores the study leveraged Voice and Accountability, Control of Corruption, Political Stability, Regional category (bloc), and GDP to predict PISAS achievement class (Low/Medium/High), finding that governance signals jointly operate with regional-bloc differentiation to distinguish achievement profiles. This indicates that science-focused sustainable education policy may benefit from governance strengthening alongside regionally informed benchmarking and institutional diffusion, while noting that the study’s country-level SHAP explanations reflect model associations rather than causal intervention effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study reframes PISA performance as country-level structural profiles by predicting Low/Medium/High achievement classes for PISA Mathematics (PISAM), Reading (PISAR), and Science (PISAS) using governance quality, economic capacity, democracy, and regional/bloc indicators. For each domain, the authors trained Random Forest and XGBoost models after two-stage feature selection (greedy correlation elimination with |r| ≥ 0.90 and VIF filtering with VIF > 7.0), then selected XGBoost as the best-performing model. Classification quality was high: class-wise Precision/Recall/F1 were mostly above 0.90, with Train Accuracy = 1.0 and Test Accuracy around 0.93–0.95, and ROC-AUC reported in the 0.98–1.00 range. Explanations were produced with SHAP and quantitatively validated using Fidelity and Faithfulness (PISAM 0.95/0.85; PISAR 0.89/0.92; PISAS 0.89/0.89). Limitations include the use of aggregate country indicators (no within-country heterogeneity) and the fact that SHAP-based attributions are predictive/explanatory associations, not causal effects; additionally, the paper does not provide a formal PV-based or survey-weighting protocol.
